summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining an ID matching their presentation, which makes every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, a potential site of distress and discrimination. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation, with the supporting rights group indicating an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025. Pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people subject to military service.

Hostility is organised rather than incidental. Anti-gender movement activity rose through 2024 and 2025, with organisations promoting the anti-trans policy positions of the United States and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Facilities are a documented friction point. The Ministry of Environment committed NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and 17% of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination said it occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. A November 2025 audit by an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.

Statutory protection exists on several fronts. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, and employment discrimination has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 of 24 May 2017 held that the constitutional grounds of discrimination are illustrative rather than exhaustive, bringing sexual orientation within the right to equality.

A Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018 effectively banned conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.
tangentialFactors:
Public visibility is high and growing. The 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, including international participants, with calls for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

Analysts describe Taiwan as among the more progressive jurisdictions in Asia for LGBT rights and the most liberal of the Chinese diaspora, a comparison that sets expectations higher than the ID regime delivers.

The wider anti-gender climate has measurable spillover. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question banning LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools and rejected the pro-inclusion question; suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults, in the aftermath. An earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform announced in March 2010 and effective in 2011 had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after opposition.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000; the Gender Equity Education Act carries a NT$100,000 fine for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment, and sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties were added in June 2011.

Following the 2018 referendum, the Education Minister said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, constraining school curricula for residents and their children.

The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. Same-sex couples can adopt, with full adoption rights legislated from May 2023 replacing the stepchild-only rights in place since 2019; single individuals, including LGBT people, may also adopt depending on circumstances.

Conversion therapy is effectively prohibited by the 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the appeal flagged after the August 2024 Taipei court ruling on ID marker change is unresolved in the available sources; no later judgment is sourced.

The scope, timing and content of the pending conscription-criteria changes referenced for 2025 are not specified in the sources, and their effect on trans draftees is unverified.

Whether the 2008 executive order has been amended, and whether any legislative bill to replace the surgical requirement has been tabled, is not sourced here.

A source page dedicated to Taiwan's transgender rights laws, protections and gaps was unavailable at research time (HTTP 404), so gaps in the legal framework are documented only through the other sources.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, complaint-handling outcomes under the employment and education statutes, or detention and policing practice toward trans people.
